tapeLine: US stocks rallied into the weekend: the S&P 500 rose 0.51% to 7,743.41, the Dow jumped 478.64 points (0.93%) to 51,828.62 — snapping a three-week losing streak — and the Nasdaq Composite added 0.5% to 27,068.72, all posting a second straight weekly gain, per CNBC and Yahoo Finance. The rally came even as the 10-year Treasury yield climbed to 5.18%, its highest close since the 2007-08 financial crisis, per the Washington Post and Post-Gazette. Oil fell as Iran floated a seven-day roadmap at the UN General Assembly to reopen the Strait of Hormuz: WTI settled down 2.33% at $92.41 and Brent down 2.14% at $104.32, per CNBC and the Washington Times. Durable goods orders were essentially flat in August, down $0.1bn to $338.6bn following July's 0.9% gain, though orders excluding transportation rose 0.3%, per the Census Bureau. The University of Michigan's final September sentiment reading rose to 48.1, a four-month low, with one-year inflation expectations jumping to 4.6% from August's 4.0%, the steepest since June, per the University of Michigan survey. Over the weekend President Trump rejected Iran's Hormuz proposal as "not acceptable," saying Tehran had "outsmarted themselves," per Fox News and the Washington Post, and the Saudi-led coalition intercepted a fresh round of Houthi missiles and drones Saturday, per Al Jazeera and The National. Futures pointed sharply lower ahead of Monday's open as WTI crude jumped as much as 4% to a session peak of $96.44 and the 10-year yield rose toward 5.23% on reports that US-Iran talks have stalled, per Investrade's Monday morning preview.
matters:
Friday's rally reads as relief, not reversal: stocks closed higher and posted a second straight weekly gain even as the 10-year Treasury yield pushed to its highest close since the 2007-08 financial crisis, at 5.18%, per the Washington Post and Post-Gazette. The Fed-hike thread this brief has carried since 18 September stayed unresolved rather than confirmed: Friday's own data was mixed, with durable goods orders essentially flat in August (-$0.1bn to $338.6bn, ex-transportation +0.3%) and the University of Michigan's final September sentiment reading edging up to 48.1 — a four-month low — even as one-year inflation expectations jumped to 4.6% from August's 4.0%, the steepest reading since June, per the Census Bureau and University of Michigan.

The Iran diplomacy thread resolved differently than the last two briefs framed it. No Trump-Pezeshkian meeting has occurred, but Iran made its most concrete move yet Friday, presenting a seven-day roadmap at the UN General Assembly — transmitted via Qatari mediators — to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the conflict in exchange for release of frozen funds, an end to oil sanctions, and an end to the US naval blockade, per the Washington Post, NPR and Al Jazeera. Some of Friday's equity rally and oil's pullback reflected that optimism, per CNBC and the Washington Times. It did not survive the weekend: President Trump rejected the proposal Saturday as "not acceptable," telling reporters Iran had "outsmarted themselves" by closing the strait and was now short of money, per Fox News; Iran said it is still awaiting a "definitive" US response despite the public rejection, per CNN.

The Houthi-Saudi front stayed active rather than escalating further: the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two ballistic missiles and two drones fired toward Khamis Mushait and the Riyadh area on Saturday, and a coalition spokesman warned further attacks would be met with a response, per Al Jazeera and The National. No new strike on Saudi energy infrastructure has been reported since Thursday's attack on Aramco facilities in Yanbu.

The financing-desk thread open since Baldwin Group on 14 September carried into the weekend without resolution: CVC and NSSK's roughly $3.2bn (JPY500bn) preliminary, non-binding proposal for Kobayashi Pharmaceutical remains just that — no financing structure has been disclosed and Kobayashi says no decision has been made, per the Japan Times and Nippon.com.

Invalidation: Monday's Dallas Fed manufacturing index (10:30 ET), any formal US response to Iran's Hormuz proposal or confirmation that talks have collapsed, and any further Houthi strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure are the next scheduled tests.
alsoOnTape: Iran said Sunday it is still awaiting a "definitive" US response on the Hormuz proposal despite Trump's public rejection, per CNN; no bombing campaign or further US military action has been confirmed. The Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish armed forces chiefs met in Riyadh on Friday to discuss military cooperation, per regional reporting. This brief could not source a confirmed Monday cash-market open at publish time; figures above are Friday's close and Monday's pre-market indications only.

flow: Friday's tape was a broad-based relief rally rather than a rotation: all three major indexes rose and posted second straight weekly gains even as the 10-year Treasury yield hit a fresh post-2008 closing high, per CNBC and the Washington Post.

regime.tag: Friday closed the week firmer on Hormuz-reopening optimism that did not survive the weekend: Trump rejected Iran's proposal Saturday, and Monday's futures point sharply lower as oil jumps and yields push further into post-2008 territory.
regime.sizing: The Fed-hike thread this brief has carried since 18 September stayed open rather than resolved: Friday's durable-goods and consumer-sentiment data were mixed, with inflation expectations rising even as headline sentiment ticked up, leaving the 28 October FOMC as the actual decision point. The Iran diplomacy thread produced its most concrete move yet — a formal seven-day roadmap to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, presented at the UN General Assembly — and its most concrete rejection, within 24 hours, which is the fastest this brief has seen a stated Iran-US proposal die. The Houthi-Saudi front held at its Thursday level (intercepted, not escalated further) rather than either resolving or spreading. The financing-desk thread stayed exactly where Friday left it: Kobayashi's preliminary approach with no disclosed financing.

secondOrder: The speed of the reversal is the notable thing here: Friday's rally and oil pullback partly priced in Iran's Hormuz-reopening proposal as a genuine de-escalation, and that pricing did not last a full weekend before Trump's rejection and Monday's sharply lower futures undid it, per Investrade. That fragility says more about how much of Friday's move was Iran-related optimism versus underlying strength than either figure could show alone. Separately, the market's ability to rally Friday despite a fresh post-2008 high in the 10-year suggests investors are treating the yield move as a known, priced-in story rather than a fresh shock — a different reaction than Wednesday's yield-driven selloff drew from the same underlying move. On the financing desk, Kobayashi's proposal has now sat non-binding for four days without disclosed terms, which is itself information: absent a firmer signal, this brief is not treating it as evidence that debt-financed sponsor buyouts are returning.

scorecard.text: Friday's brief flagged any escalation or de-escalation around the Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia as a next test. The front stayed active: the Saudi-led coalition intercepted two ballistic missiles and two drones aimed at Khamis Mushait and the Riyadh area on Saturday, and a coalition spokesman warned that further attacks would be met with a response, per Al Jazeera and The National.

Friday's brief again flagged any sign of a Trump-Pezeshkian meeting as a next test; no meeting has occurred. Instead, Iran presented a formal seven-day roadmap to reopen the Strait of Hormuz at the UN General Assembly Friday, which Trump rejected Saturday as "not acceptable" — a more concrete development than the meeting question itself, but the meeting remains unscheduled and the underlying US-Iran talks are reported stalled as of Monday's premarket.
